disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes accompanied by delusions and/or hallucinations that are present only during the mood episode. The psychotic content is often mood-congruent, involving themes of guilt, worthlessness, illness, or deserved punishment, and can significantly worsen distress and impairment. Clinically, patients present with the full depressive syndrome plus fixed false beliefs or sensory experiences that are not shared by others, yet feel vividly real to them. It is distinguished from primary psychotic disorders by the temporal linkage of psychosis to depressive episodes and the absence of a history of independent manic or hypomanic episodes that would suggest bipolar disorder.

narrative.stressor: About a year and a half ago, James underwent a minor cardiac procedure after an episode of chest discomfort, which led his doctors and family to strongly limit his driving, heavy lifting, and some of his more physical volunteer duties at the senior center and church. Losing these roles disrupted the carefully structured routine he had followed for decades and left him spending long stretches of time alone at home while his wife managed her own emerging mobility issues. Over the following year, he gradually pulled back from bowling, bridge, and even coordinating volunteers, telling himself he was "too old" to be useful, while privately ruminating about whether he was becoming a burden. His pastor and a long-time bowling friend finally urged his wife to bring him to a psychiatrist when he began insisting, with unshakable conviction, that his past mistakes had irreparably harmed his family and that he "ought" to be punished, despite reassurance and lack of evidence from those around him.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t shake this feeling that I’ve ruined everything for my family and don’t deserve to be here anymore, no matter what anyone tells me.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly fourteen months ago, Josephine transitioned from an internship-style role into a full-time engineering technician position on a high-visibility aerospace project with tight deadlines and a demanding supervisor. Initially she coped by doubling down on her usual meticulous routines—late nights refining CAD models, weekend troubleshooting of 3-D printed components, and volunteering for extra tasks to prove herself. Over time, the workload and a perfectionistic internal standard eroded her boundaries: she stopped running with her track club, skipped board-game nights, and began spending most evenings alone in her apartment reviewing work in her head instead of resting. When she started to notice that she was no longer enjoying her technical hobbies and that she was making small but consequential mistakes at work because she could not focus on even simple schematics, her manager suggested the employee assistance program, which led to a psychiatric referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I used to be able to focus for hours on designs, but now my mind feels foggy and I can’t make even basic decisions at work.”

narrative.stressor: About a year and a few months ago, John’s father died unexpectedly from a myocardial infarction back in Indonesia, and John was unable to travel for the funeral because of visa logistics and rigid staffing needs at his clinic. The combination of grief, guilt over not being present for his family, and the daily exposure to patients with cardiac and terminal illnesses at work created a constant backdrop of loss that he tried to manage by working longer hours and volunteering at more community health fairs. As the months passed, close colleagues noticed that his usual balance between structured care and self-care had collapsed: he stopped joining hikes, let his photography and cooking fall away, and increasingly kept to himself even during breaks, seeming preoccupied and withdrawn. He finally agreed to seek psychiatric help after confiding to a fellow physician that he was convinced his patients would be better off without him and had started to dwell repeatedly on the idea that he would be "relieved" if he simply did not wake up, prompting his colleague to insist on an urgent evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep thinking everyone would be better off if I just weren’t here anymore, and these thoughts about not wanting to wake up won’t stop.”
